newsitem.title: MONACO: OLYMPICS-IOC PROBE SEOUL BOXING SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC PROBE SEOUL BOXING SCANDAL.

text.p: The boxing scandal of the 1988 Seoul Games could be resolved this week when the International Olympic Committee probe allegations of corruption and cheating.
Accusations that American light-middleweight Roy Jones missed out on a gold medal because of bribed judges were believed to have been discussed at a meeting of IOC legal experts on Monday.
The officials were expected to put their views to the IOC's ruling executive board which opened a three-day meeting later.
Last year, the IOC appointed a commission to investigate the alleged corruption involving a number of ringside judges in Seoul.

One report on the affair, including documents obtained from the archives of former East Germany's secret police which took a great interest in sport, alleges somes judges were bribed in favour of South Koreans and certain international boxing officials were aware of the cheating.
Jones, who went on to become a professional world champion, was beaten in the 1988 final by South Korean Park Si-hun after an extraordinary decision.
Most spectators and commentators present had Jones way ahead of his outclassed opponent but three judges from Morocco, Uruguay and Uganda gave the decision to Park.
Last March, the IOC said it needed to talk to one key figure in the affair before it could announce the result of its findings. But it expected its final report to be ready in May.
At a time when more and more athletes are taking their disputes with sporting authorities to the civil courts, Olympic chiefs know they must take a decision which is legally watertight.

On Monday, members of the IOC's juridical commission refused even to confirm that they had discussed the matter. But one Olympic source said their recommendations would almost certainly be discussed during the executive board meeting.
